title: Explain the useful idea without its name.
question: How can one reading help us recover two?
body: Two temperature sensors record a room. Their paired readings form a narrow cloud. Explain to someone who understands a ruler, but has not learned vectors, how a shared line and one distance can give an approximate pair of readings.
takeaway: A clear explanation keeps the purpose, the reconstruction, and the lost detail.
prompt: Write or sketch your explanation. Include what we store once, what we store for each observation, and one detail that could disappear. Then answer: if two dots land at the same place on the line, were their original readings necessarily identical?
rubric: Names the shared line and its anchor as part of the decoding rule.
Explains that each observation supplies one signed position on the line.
Distinguishes the recovered pair from the original pair.
Answers the follow-up: different dots can share a projection, so the shorter description can lose detail.
example: Choose one line through the middle of the dots and keep it as a shared ruler. For each dot, save where it lands on that ruler. Later, that position gives us a nearby pair of readings. We lose how far the original dot lay sideways from the ruler. Two different dots can land at the same position, so the saved number cannot always tell them apart.
notes: [Leave the example hidden.] This is a translation task, not a test of whether you remember the term principal component. Imagine one listener who knows what a ruler and a dot are. Tell that listener what the shorter message lets us do. [Pause for an explanation.] Now ask the follow-up about two dots landing together. If the explanation cannot answer it, add the missing lost detail. Compare your answer with the rubric, not with the wording of the example. A different clear explanation can work. This lens assumes a particular starting knowledge; it does not set a limit based on anyone's age.

title: Turn that explanation into a calculation.
question: Can a negative direction still give a useful score?
body: The stored mean is (20, 20) °C. The shared unit direction is w = (1, −1)/√2. A new pair of readings is (22, 19) °C. Center the pair, calculate its score, and recover a pair in the original temperature units.
takeaway: Center first, project, then add the stored mean when decoding.
prompt: Show the centered point, score, recovered pair, and squared gap. Explain each to the listener from the previous scene. Follow-up: replacing w by −w changes which results?
rubric: Centers to (2, −1), using the stored mean rather than a new single-observation mean.
Calculates z = 3/√2 and the recovered pair (21.5, 18.5) °C.
Finds residual (0.5, 0.5) and squared Euclidean gap 0.5 °C².
Explains that reversing w reverses the score but preserves the decoded point and error.
example: The deviations are (2, −1). Their signed projection is (2 + 1)/√2 = 3/√2. Multiplying by w gives (1.5, −1.5); adding the mean gives (21.5, 18.5). The missed part is (0.5, 0.5), whose squared length is 0.5. If both direction and score change sign, their product stays the same.
notes: [Point to the stored mean before the direction.] These are temperatures, so the origin of our ruler matters. Subtracting twenty from each reading measures a deviation from the learned center. The second coefficient is negative because this direction represents a contrast between the sensors. It does not mean a negative temperature is required. [Pause before revealing the answer.] Once you have a score, reverse the process: multiply by the direction and put the center back. Now reverse the arrow. The coordinate changes sign, but the recovered point does not move. Explain that cancellation in ordinary language as well as symbols.

title: Explain why this matrix belongs here.
question: Can you derive covariance from the task?
body: Consider four sensor pairs: (22,19), (21,18), (19,22), (18,21). Their mean is (20,20). A proposed summary reports both sample variances as 10/3 but omits their covariance. Explain what that summary cannot tell us.
takeaway: The mixed term connects the direction's spread to how the measurements vary together.
prompt: Expand the square of z = w₁u + w₂v for centered coordinates u and v. Sum over the four observations, divide by n−1, and build C. Use the sign of its off-diagonal entry to explain the useful tilt. Follow-up: is negative covariance evidence that C has a negative eigenvalue?
rubric: Includes the cross term 2w₁w₂uv.
Obtains C = [[10, −8], [−8, 10]]/3 and maps each entry to a sum of products.
Connects Var(z) to wᵀCw rather than presenting C as an unexplained recipe.
Explains that negative covariance is allowed while wᵀCw remains nonnegative; positive semidefinite does not mean every entry is positive.
example: Squaring the score gives w₁²u² + 2w₁w₂uv + w₂²v². Here the sums of u² and v² are both 10, while the sum of uv is −8. Dividing by three gives C. Opposite signs in w make the mixed contribution positive, favoring a falling diagonal. For every w, wᵀCw is a sum of squared scores divided by three, so it cannot be negative.
notes: [Keep the final matrix hidden while the learner expands the square.] The two separate variances are the same as in a rising cloud, so they cannot tell us which diagonal matters. We need the products that record how the two deviations occur together. Have the learner trace one matrix entry back to the four observations. Then ask why the same matrix works for every proposed direction. The coefficients change with the ruler; the stored sums do not. The final follow-up separates a negative relationship from a negative variance. A matrix can contain negative entries while every projected variance is nonnegative. That is the meaning of positive semidefinite here.

title: Rebuild the argument without the slides.
question: Why is the leading direction globally best?
body: Use a centered data matrix X with observations as rows and C = XᵀX/(n−1). Start from squared reconstruction error on a line. End with a bound that covers every unit direction. Name any theorem you invoke.
takeaway: A complete argument connects the loss, the covariance matrix, the stationary candidates, and the global bound.
prompt: Reconstruct the proof in your own order, but justify every arrow. Include why the direction has unit length, why centering matters for variance, why Cw = λw alone is insufficient, and when equality holds in the final bound. Then explain the same argument using the ruler and its lost sideways detail.
rubric: Defines score wᵀxᵢ and reconstruction w(wᵀxᵢ) with ||w|| = 1.
Uses orthogonality to write total squared residual as fixed total squared length minus squared-score sum.
Uses zero score mean to identify retained sample variance as wᵀCw.
Derives Cw = λw as a stationary condition and notes that a minimum also satisfies it.
Invokes the symmetric spectral theorem, expands w = Σaⱼqⱼ, and uses Σaⱼ² = 1.
Justifies cross terms with Cqⱼ = λⱼqⱼ and orthonormality, then bounds Σλⱼaⱼ² by λmax.
States that equality means w lies in the top eigenspace, including ties, and translates the result back to reconstruction.
example: For a unit w, the projection and residual are perpendicular. Thus error equals a fixed total minus Σ(wᵀxᵢ)². Centering makes the projected mean zero, so maximizing that sum is maximizing wᵀCw. A constrained derivative gives Cw = λw, which only identifies candidates. Because C is symmetric, take an orthonormal eigenbasis. Every unit w has coefficients whose squares sum to one. Its variance is Σλⱼaⱼ² ≤ λmax, with equality in the top eigenspace. That direction therefore minimizes the original squared reconstruction error.
notes: [Close notes and previous equations for the first attempt.] This is a reconstruction task, so allow time to write, draw, or speak the chain before opening the example. If a step is missing, identify its job: defining the allowed ruler, measuring loss, summarizing the data, finding candidates, or ruling out every better direction. Do not repair the whole proof for the learner. Offer the smallest missing connection, then ask for a fresh attempt. Pay special attention to the stationary condition. It cannot choose the maximum by itself. Finally, translate the proof back into the original geometry. Successful symbol manipulation should still explain what is recovered and what is lost.

title: A different answer can be equally correct.
question: What is unique when eigenvalues tie?
body: A four-feature covariance matrix has eigenvalues 9, 4, 4, 1. You keep k = 2 directions. Two programs agree on the first direction but choose different second directions inside the eigenvalue-4 plane.
takeaway: A tie across the retained boundary can make the optimal subspace nonunique.
prompt: Choose a conclusion, then justify it with the top-k objective. Follow-up: what changes if k = 3? State the retained and discarded variance in both cases.
choices: At most one program can be correct because PCA has one fixed answer.
Both can be optimal at k = 2; at k = 3 the leading subspace is unique although its basis need not be.
Any pair of perpendicular directions is optimal because two eigenvalues tie.
feedback: The tie allows different choices inside its eigenspace. Compare subspaces and objectives, not just individual arrays.
Yes. For k = 2, retain 9 + 4 = 13 and discard 5. For k = 3, retain 17 and discard 1; the gap from 4 to 1 separates that full leading subspace.
The eigenvalue-9 direction must still be retained to reach 13. Orthogonality alone does not guarantee the maximum.
rubric: Uses the sum of the largest k eigenvalues as the captured-variance optimum.
Explains the boundary tie at k = 2 and the separated boundary at k = 3.
Distinguishes freedom to rotate a basis within a subspace from changing the retained subspace.
Reports residual variance 5 for k = 2 and 1 for k = 3, not an unnormalized sum of squared errors.
example: At k = 2 we must keep the eigenvalue-9 direction and may choose any unit direction in the eigenvalue-4 plane. Different choices give different optimal two-dimensional subspaces with captured variance 13. At k = 3 we retain that entire plane, giving one leading three-dimensional subspace and captured variance 17. Its basis remains nonunique inside the tied plane.
notes: [Ask for a reason before selecting an option.] A numerical comparison can flag two different arrays even when both solve the same problem. Here the tie sits exactly at the two-component cutoff, so the ambiguity concerns the retained subspace itself. Now change the cutoff to three. We retain the whole tied plane, and the next eigenvalue is smaller. The leading subspace is then fixed, while a basis within it can still rotate. Use the follow-up to separate those two claims. This also explains why a near tie can make individual directions sensitive to small changes. Stability of a retained subspace depends on the gap at its own boundary.

title: Zero covariance can hide a rule.
question: Do uncorrelated scores have to be independent?
body: Let Z take −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 with equal probability. Set A = Z and B = Z² − 2. Both have mean zero. Positive and negative values of Z cancel in E[AB], so the covariance is zero.
takeaway: Decorrelation removes a linear summary of dependence, not every possible relationship.
prompt: What follows? After selecting, explain how learning A = 0 changes what we know about B. Then say exactly which dependence claim PCA can justify for its training scores.
choices: A and B are independent because their covariance is zero.
A and B are dependent even though the coordinate covariance is diagonal.
A covariance matrix cannot describe these variables because their relationship is nonlinear.
feedback: If A = 0, then B must be −2. Knowing A changes the distribution of B, so they are dependent.
Correct. B is a deterministic function of A. A diagonal covariance records zero cross-covariance, which is a weaker statement.
Covariance is defined here and is useful, but it does not summarize the full nonlinear relationship.
rubric: Uses a conditional fact, such as A = 0 implies B = −2, to show dependence.
Explains the cancellation in E[Z(Z²−2)] using symmetry.
States that PCA scores along an orthonormal eigenbasis are uncorrelated in the fitted data.
Does not promote zero sample covariance into general population independence.
example: Knowing A fixes B, so the variables are dependent. Their covariance still vanishes because odd powers of symmetric Z average to zero. PCA can diagonalize a covariance matrix; it cannot remove this deterministic curve merely by making a linear change of coordinates. Independence would need additional assumptions or evidence.
notes: [Have the learner predict B when A is zero.] This one conditional question is enough to challenge the claim of independence. We do not need a complicated dependence measure. The covariance vanishes because positive and negative contributions cancel, not because the variables have nothing to do with each other. Ask the learner to explain why both statements can be true. Then return to PCA. Perpendicular directions and zero cross-covariance of the fitted scores are precise achievements. They do not identify independent causes or eliminate nonlinear relations. Keep the distinction between the finite dataset used to fit PCA and a broader population that we hope the data represents.

title: Audit the claim behind a clean plot.
question: What evidence would turn a pattern into a useful finding?
body: A report says: “Our first two PCs retain 92% of the variance and separate two groups, so we found the two causes of the system.” The report fitted preprocessing and PCA on all observations before evaluating later observations.
takeaway: A sample reconstruction guarantee does not establish causes, stability, or future task performance.
prompt: Separate what the report may have demonstrated from its unsupported claims. Propose two discriminating checks and explain what each check can and cannot establish. Follow-up: can a stable PCA axis still reflect an irrelevant nuisance?
rubric: Recognizes 92% as retained variance in the chosen fitted representation, not a causal or predictive percentage.
Identifies that fitting preprocessing on evaluation observations contaminates an out-of-sample comparison.
Proposes a train-only, task-appropriate evaluation and a distinct stability or nuisance check.
States that stability does not establish causal meaning or relevance, and limits any causal conclusion to an appropriate research design.
example: The fit may show that a two-dimensional subspace reconstructs this processed sample with a small relative squared-error tail. Refit preprocessing and PCA on training observations only, then evaluate the declared task on untouched later data. Separately perturb or resample the training data and compare subspaces, while checking known nuisance variables. Those checks assess generalization and stability; neither alone proves that the components are causes.
notes: [Separate the numerical statement from the scientific conclusion.] A correct calculation can support a much narrower claim than its headline. Ask which data, units, preprocessing, and objective the ninety-two percent belongs to. Then inspect the evaluation timeline. Even an unsupervised transformation learns from its input, so including future evaluation data can change the representation. Finally, ask what a stable direction means. A repeated nuisance, such as instrument setting, can be very stable. The learner should propose tests that could disconfirm their preferred interpretation and say what uncertainty survives. This scene practices research judgment; it does not claim that one course supplies a complete causal-inference method.

title: Design a fair comparison.
question: Which smaller description serves this task?
body: A sensor archive must support both compression and fault prediction. A large shared temperature swing dominates variance. A small contrast between sensors carries the fault label. Compare one-PC compression, a choice of more PCs, and a regularized predictor using the original features.
takeaway: Judge methods against their intended losses, with shared evaluation conditions.
prompt: Specify the hypotheses, data split, fitted preprocessing, candidate choices, and two outcome measures. State what result would change your recommendation. Explain the comparison to a colleague who knows the sensor task but has never heard of PCA.
rubric: Measures reconstruction quality and predictive performance separately, using suitable units and losses.
Fits every learned transformation within the training portion of the evaluation design.
Chooses component count and regularization without using the final held-out outcomes.
Uses the same observations and practical constraints for competing methods, while stating their different objectives.
Gives a result that could overturn the preferred method and explains the tradeoff in ordinary language.
example: Use training and validation periods to choose the retained dimension and predictor settings, then evaluate once on a later untouched period. Compare reconstruction error per feature and a fault-prediction loss suitable for the error costs. One PC may compress well while losing the fault contrast; more PCs or the original-feature predictor may preserve it. I would change the recommendation if the extra predictive value fails to persist in the held-out period or costs more storage or complexity than the application permits.
notes: [Ask the learner to name the two decisions before naming algorithms.] A single score cannot automatically settle both compression and fault detection. First define what the archive must recover and which prediction mistakes matter. Then plan how choices will be made without looking at the final evaluation outcomes. Keep a simple baseline in the comparison; an advanced method must earn its cost. Ask for the result that would change the recommendation, because a study designed only to confirm a favored method is weak evidence. Finish with the plain-language explanation. A research-level comparison should remain connected to the operational question that motivated it.

title: Translate the warning without losing the idea.
question: Can you explain why a good compression can miss a fault?
body: Return to the listener who knows a ruler but not covariance. The sensor cloud is long in one direction. Two fault states differ only by a small sideways shift. Explain why the best one-number reconstruction can hide that shift.
takeaway: Simplifying the language should preserve the relation between the objective and its boundary.
prompt: Give an explanation of no more than six sentences, with a sketch if helpful. Avoid “eigenvector,” “variance,” and “dimensionality.” Include the useful part of the method and its limit. Follow-up from the listener: “Then why not always keep the tiny direction instead?”
rubric: Explains that the main ruler keeps the large changes and gives small average reconstruction gaps.
Shows that the small sideways fault change can disappear in the saved coordinate.
Answers that the better direction depends on the question: recovering readings and detecting faults need not prefer the same one.
Offers a response such as keeping another coordinate or testing a method aimed at the fault task, without calling PCA universally bad.
example: The long ruler keeps the biggest movements in our readings. Most recovered dots then sit close to their originals. But the fault moves a dot a little sideways, and that small move disappears when we save only its place on the ruler. Keeping the sideways direction could help detect the fault, while losing more of the large temperature changes. We should choose what to keep based on what we need to do, or keep both if the space allows.
notes: [Keep the model explanation hidden until the learner answers the follow-up.] This is the return journey from technical reasoning to ordinary language. Removing hard words is not enough: the explanation must still connect the task, the chosen rule, and the missed detail. Ask the listener's question about keeping the tiny direction instead. A strong answer does not defend PCA at all costs. It explains that different questions can need different summaries. If the learner can only say that important information was lost, ask them to draw the two fault states and show exactly where that difference goes. Then try the explanation again in their own words.

title: A cutoff must answer the analysis question.
question: Would you discard a small but useful component?
body: In Seurat's documented single-cell example, later PCs can reflect rare immune subsets. Imagine that the first ten PCs reach your chosen variance threshold, but a later PC highlights markers relevant to the rare population you want to study.
takeaway: A variance threshold is a compression choice; it is not a guarantee that every relevant group survives.
prompt: Choose the next action and explain the evidence you would seek. Follow-up: why is keeping every later PC also not an automatic solution?
choices: Discard the later PC because the variance threshold settles biological relevance.
Declare a new cell type from the PCA plot alone.
Inspect the contributing features and compare downstream results across justified component counts.
feedback: Total variance can be dominated by common variation. A rare signal can matter to the stated analysis despite a small variance share.
A visualization can suggest a question, but biological interpretation needs supporting evidence and checks for technical effects.
Yes. Inspect what the component represents and test sensitivity to the cutoff; additional components may also introduce unwanted variation.
rubric: States the specific rare-population objective instead of treating retained variance as the only outcome.
Requests feature/loading evidence and checks plausible technical explanations.
Compares downstream results across reasonable component counts.
Explains the cost of keeping additional noise or nuisance variation and avoids inferring a biological cause from a plot.
example: Inspect the genes associated with the later PC, seek domain evidence for the proposed population, and check technical covariates. Repeat the relevant downstream analysis with several component counts and assess whether the finding persists. Keeping every component can reintroduce technical variation, so the choice still requires evidence rather than a fixed universal cutoff.
notes: [State that this is an interpretation exercise, not a complete single-cell protocol.] The documented Seurat workflow makes component count a decision and encourages checking how later choices affect results. That is the lesson to transfer. A small component can reflect a rare population, but it can also reflect an unwanted technical effect. Ask the learner what evidence distinguishes those possibilities. Then ask why retaining everything is not automatically better. The answer should connect back to the purpose of compression and noise reduction, while acknowledging their assumptions. Do not let a visually distinct group stand in for a validated biological finding.

title: Make a plan you could actually test.
question: Where would PCA earn a place in your workflow?
body: Choose a small dataset you understand, or use the temperature-sensor case. Write a plan before fitting PCA. Define what each row and feature means, what a shorter representation should preserve, and what evidence would make you reject it.
takeaway: A useful application plan ties preprocessing, component count, and validation to one declared purpose.
prompt: Specify: purpose; rows and features; units and preprocessing; fitting/evaluation split; component-count rule; baseline; success measure; one failure diagnostic; and the next action if that diagnostic fails. Finish by explaining your choice to a teammate in three plain sentences.
rubric: Defines the data axes and a concrete task rather than saying only reduce dimensions.
Justifies centering and any feature scaling in terms of the chosen loss.
Fits learned preprocessing and PCA on training data and uses an appropriate held-out evaluation.
Compares with a meaningful simple baseline and states a task-specific success measure.
Names one mechanism of failure, an observable diagnostic, and a response with its remaining cost.
example: For a sensor archive, each row is a time observation and columns are calibrated temperatures in the same units. Fit the center and PCA on an earlier period, choose k on a validation period for a reconstruction-error budget, and compare with keeping raw readings. Evaluate later data and inspect per-sensor residuals and fault performance separately. If a small fault contrast disappears, increase k or use a task-specific representation; that costs storage or extra modeling.
notes: [Ask for the purpose in one sentence first.] A plan becomes testable when another person can tell what success and failure would look like. Check the data axes before the method: a transposed matrix changes what observations and directions mean. Then examine the units, because they define the error we are minimizing. Ask where each learned quantity is fitted and how the retained dimension is chosen. Finally, request one failure and a concrete response. The plan does not need to use PCA to pass this task. A well-supported decision to keep the original features can be the best outcome.

title: Come back and rebuild it.
question: What can you reconstruct after the explanation is no longer fresh?
body: On a later day, start with a blank page and keep the model answers closed. Draw a new cloud, explain one-number encoding, rebuild the covariance-to-global-optimum argument, and invent a case in which the best reconstruction misses the task.
takeaway: Use a later independent attempt to find what needs repair; completion today is not evidence of lasting recall.
prompt: Save a short prompt for your later self: “Why covariance? Why an eigenvector? Why the largest? Best for what?” Answer it without this course, then reopen only the bridge you could not justify. After repair, try a different dataset or explanation recipient. What question would you now investigate beyond this course?
rubric: Records which claims were reconstructed unaided and which required help, without treating either as a score assigned by the app.
Recovers the purpose-to-loss-to-covariance-to-global-bound chain.
Supplies a changed-case boundary rather than only repeating the original example.
Explains the core to a less-prepared listener while preserving the chosen objective and one limitation.
States a bounded next research or application question and the evidence needed to address it.
example: My reconstruction should connect a shared line and score to lost squared distance, show why covariance summarizes the score variance, distinguish stationarity from the global eigenvalue bound, and state that this optimum concerns a chosen metric. A next investigation might test whether a later low-variance component improves a particular held-out task. Any missing bridge becomes a focused repair task, followed by a new unaided attempt.
notes: [Do not reveal the example until the learner has saved their own return prompt.] This scene sets a future challenge; it does not claim that later recall has been measured, and it does not schedule a reminder. Choose a later opportunity when the learner can begin without rereading. Ask them to mark where their reasoning stopped, not to hide that gap with familiar terminology. Reopen the relevant bridge, repair it, and then change the case so the next attempt is more than copying. End with a question the learner can now investigate responsibly. The useful result is ownership of an argument and a decision process, not a claim of universal expertise.
